name: Midnight navy
lede: Midnight navy is a near-black blue that compounds two familiar color words, midnight and navy, the second of them pointing to naval uniform blue rather than any single document our library records a date for.

sections.title: Two borrowed words
sections.body:
Our library carries no dated first record for this exact compound name, only its Munsell notation, 5.4PB 1.3/2.9, and the ISCC-NBS block it falls in, a dark blue 7.3 units from that block's center [1]. Navy blue as a color word is tied to naval uniforms: a dark blue became the standard color of British Royal Navy officers' coats from the mid-eighteenth century on, and the word for the color followed the word for the service [3]. Midnight simply names the hour, used across many color names for the darkest member of a family, such as [[midnight-blue]] and [[midnight-purple]].

The nearest named colors on file are [[mascot]], [[dark]] and [[black-blue]], at 4.1, 4.1 and 4.6 ΔE [3]. It is several shades darker than the plain name [[navy]] and sits beside [[dark-navy]] and [[deep-navy]] in the same small family [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of Midnight navy covers at least five percent of the canvas in 193 works, about eight tenths of one percent [2]. The earliest dated example is Pietro Lorenzetti's 1340 altarpiece of the Madonna and Child enthroned with eight angels, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2]. It peaks in the 1920s, in 7 of 237 paintings, more than three and a half times the archive's overall rate for that decade [2]. Ninety-six percent of its appearances fall in a painting's shadows rather than its mid-tones or highlights[2]. It shares a canvas with the plain name [[navy]] far more than chance, thirty-four times the baseline [2]. These are screen-color matches on photographs of aged, varnished paintings, never a claim about pigment [2]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, read as screen colors, not pigment identifications[2].
